key_claims: A composition on Rock 29, on the upper terrace of Boyukdash at Gobustan, 'may preserve something far more specific than a generic scene of prehistoric life'.
That composition has four elements: a large oared vessel, water-like markings, armed figures moving across rough ground, and an unusual raised terminal at one end of the boat.

Taken together these raise the question (posed as a question, not asserted) whether 'the original expedition' was carved 'thousands of years before' it became the Greek story of Jason and the Argonauts.
The carving 'may preserve the voyage that Greek poets later transformed' into the myth. The wording throughout the readable portion is 'may', 'could' and a question mark.

The evidence is said to lead 'from a cave behind the engraving to a transformed Caspian shoreline and a possible route across the Caucasus'. That is a signpost for the paywalled argument; none of the three steps is argued in the readable text.

Citing Sigari: Rock 29 is a large boulder on the upper terrace of Boyuk Dash, forms the southern side of Ana Zaga cave, and is engraved on its southern, eastern and northern surfaces. The article calls this 'the crucial topographical fact'.
evidence_offered: In the readable portion: a verbal description of the Rock 29 motifs, and one quotation plus one paraphrase from Dario Sigari's study of the Gobustan boats for the rock's position against Ana Zaga cave. No photograph or tracing of the panel, no date, no measurement, no ancient text and no reference list are visible. The lead image is a Renaissance painting which the caption itself says is not evidence. Whatever supports the cave, shoreline and route steps is behind the paywall and was not read.
date_range_estimates: None given in the readable portion. For the motif: only 'thousands of years before it became Greece's most famous adventure', with no figure and no period named. The readable text does not use the words 'Bronze Age'. For the site: people 'occupied this place for thousands of years', again with no figure. No date is given for Ana Zaga cave layers or for the shoreline. [uncertain] Any specific dates in the paywalled remainder are unknown.
dating_method: None stated in the readable portion. The signpost sentence (cave behind the engraving, then a 'transformed Caspian shoreline') suggests the paywalled argument rests on association with the Ana Zaga cave and on shoreline correlation, but that is an inference from one sentence. [uncertain] The actual method used in the full article was not read.
panel_details: Rock 29 (Sigari's 'Rock No. 29'), a large boulder on the upper terrace of Boyukdash (Boyuk Dash), forming the southern side of Ana Zaga cave; engraved on its southern, eastern and northern surfaces according to the article's report of Sigari. Motifs named: one large oared vessel with 'an unusual raised terminal at one end', 'water-like markings', and 'armed figures moving across rough ground'. The article calls these 'a composition'. The readable text does not say which of the three faces carries the boat, gives no dimensions or figure counts, and says nothing about superimpositions or whether the motifs are of one period.
geographic_claims: Sea: the Caspian. The boulder is 'above the Caspian' and the terrace looks 'toward the Caspian lowlands'; the argument invokes 'a transformed Caspian shoreline'. Route: 'a possible route across the Caucasus', with no rivers, passes or endpoints named in the readable text. The Black Sea, Colchis, Phasis, Aia, the Kura (Cyrus) and Rioni are not mentioned in the readable portion. [uncertain] Which river corridor or direction of travel the full article proposes was not read.
counter_evidence: From the article itself: every claim in the readable portion is hedged ('may preserve', 'could', a question), and the caption to its own lead image disclaims evidential value. It gives no date for the boat, so 'thousands of years before' is unsupported as read. It treats boat, water marks and armed figures as one composition without showing they were made together, on a rock it says is engraved on three faces. It places the story on the Caspian, while the readable text never addresses that the myth's Colchis is on the Black Sea, beyond promising 'a possible route across the Caucasus'. The author is a retired mathematics educator with no stated rock-art or classics training and no stated fieldwork at Gobustan. The outlet is rated Low credibility and Conspiracy-Pseudoscience by Media Bias/Fact Check. Search results (not opened here) also point to a 2023 study of Ana Zaga noting superimposed figures and previously unrecorded boats on stone 29's northern side, which bears on the single-scene reading. [uncertain] That last point is from a search snippet only.
independent_corroboration: None found. Four live searches on 10 October 2026 (author name plus Gobustan and Argonauts, the article title terms, and the claim without the author's name) returned only the Ancient Origins page and its Substack mirror. No news pickup, no specialist comment, no peer-reviewed paper or preprint on the Gobustan proposal was found. The Substack post shows 14 reactions and 0 comments.
alternative_explanations: The article concedes the default reading in passing: 'a generic scene of prehistoric life' among rocks covered with images by people who lived there 'for thousands of years'. It does not engage with any specialist interpretation in the readable portion beyond using Sigari for the rock's position. Search results (not opened for this item) describe boats as one of the most frequent motifs at Gobustan, so a boat with armed figures is not distinctive in itself. [uncertain] How Sigari and others read the Rock 29 boats is for the Sigari and typology items to establish.

relevance_to_essay: This is the whole proposal, and what can be read of it is a question with a list of four motifs and one borrowed fact about where the rock sits. It shows the pattern the essay is testing: a wordless image is given a named story by assembling separate marks into one scene and then promising a chain (cave, shoreline, route) to carry it to Greece. The essay can quote the hedged wording exactly and should say plainly that the argument proper sits behind a paywall and was not read.
open_questions: What dates the full article gives for the boat, and how. What it says about Ana Zaga cave layers and the Caspian shoreline. Which route across the Caucasus it proposes and whether it deals with Colchis being on the Black Sea. Which face of Rock 29 carries the boat and what the 'raised terminal' is taken to be (the readable text does not say). Whether the Sigari quotation is accurate and in context. Whether a preprint or paper lies behind the article. Whether the author has visited Gobustan.
